I crawled the formatter section, capped at 15 pages. It only contains 2 pages: `/ruff/formatter/` and `/ruff/formatter/black/`. The full settings reference is at `/ruff/settings/#format`, which is outside that section, so I didn't read it.

**Options named in the formatter docs**

- `line-length`: maximum line width (top-level setting, not under `[format]`). The example uses 100.
- `format.quote-style`: preferred quote character for strings. The example uses `"single"`, and f-string handling refers to it.
- `format.indent-style`: spaces or tabs. The example uses `"tab"`.
- `format.docstring-code-format`: formats code examples inside docstrings (doctest, Markdown and reStructuredText).
- `format.docstring-code-line-length`: line width for those docstring code examples. The example uses 20.
- `format.nested-string-quote-style`: for Python 3.12+, `"preferred"` makes nested f-string strings use the configured quote style.
- `format.preview`: enables preview-style formatting, such as the fluent layout for method chains.
- `extension`: top-level mapping of custom file extensions to a language, for example `{ mdx = "markdown", qmd = "markdown" }`, so Markdown code blocks in those files get formatted.
- `extend-exclude`: top-level setting. The page uses it to turn off Markdown formatting with `["*.md"]`.

**CLI flags mentioned**

- `ruff format --check`: reports what would change without writing files.
- `--exit-non-zero-on-format`: exits with code 1 when files were formatted.
- `ruff format --help`: the page points to this for the full list of CLI options.

**Inline suppression comments** (not settings)

- `# fmt: off` / `# fmt: on`
- `# fmt: skip`, if the page covers it (I didn't check)
- `<!-- fmt:off -->` / `<!-- fmt:on -->` in Markdown, with `blacken-docs:off` and `blacken-docs:on` as equivalents

The page says Ruff exposes only "a small set of configuration options" and no others, and it sends readers to the settings page for the full list. That list likely includes more, such as `line-ending`, `skip-magic-trailing-comma` and `exclude`. I haven't confirmed that, and I can fetch the settings page if you want it checked.

**Vercel gives far more bandwidth on its free tier.**

| | Free plan | Bandwidth |
|---|---|---|
| **Vercel (Hobby)** | Hard usage caps | 100 GB/month of Fast Data Transfer |
| **Netlify (Free)** | 300 credits/month | At most 15 GB/month |

- **Netlify:** bandwidth isn't a fixed allowance. It is billed at 20 credits per GB out of one 300-credit pool. That pool also pays for production deploys (15 credits each), compute, and web requests. So 15 GB (300 ÷ 20) is a ceiling you'd only reach by spending nothing else.
- **Vercel:** I read the 100 GB figure from the pricing table, where it sits in the Hobby column. The scraped text doesn't label the columns, so that placement is my inference. Vercel's FAQ also says Hobby accounts are limited to the usage caps and can't buy more.

Vercel's Hobby plan is also restricted to personal, non-commercial use.

Sources: https://vercel.com/pricing and https://www.netlify.com/pricing/ (scraped fresh today).

The latest release in the changelog is **0.13.2**, released 2026-10-19. This is what it lists.

**Enhancements (the "added" items)**
- `uv workspace metadata` now reports all installed packages, including ones outside the selected resolution.
- Exporting `pylock.toml` now includes supported environment restrictions.
- Dropped GET and HEAD requests are retried when fetching package and index data.
- Encoding declarations are preserved in wheel data scripts that need shell launchers.
- `uv python find --script` shows causes and hints when it can't find an interpreter, including with `-q`.
- uv prints valid ksh activation instructions and supports non-relocatable environments under OpenBSD-derived ksh.
- uv-build's `[build-system].requires` validation now allows PEP 508 direct URLs, including Mercurial and extensionless archive URLs.

**Python**
- Adds PyPy 3.11.17 and 3.12.15.

**Preview features**
- With `wheel-variants`, uv fetches and parses PEP 825 index-level variant metadata.

**Performance**
- Complex dependency markers are simplified, traversed and exported without exponential work. They also take less time and memory to parse and store.
- The resolver uses less memory on large dependency graphs.
- Project discovery in large workspaces is faster.
- The uv and `uv-build` binaries are smaller, and CycloneDX exports are faster.
- TOML parsing makes fewer allocations.

**Bug fixes**
- Several fixes stop URL credentials leaking through diagnostics or persisted metadata.
- `--exclude-newer` is now respected when a newer wheel for the selected source distribution is already cached.
- Several fixes replace panics with proper errors, such as invalid `uv pip compile --python-version` values and invalid `pylock.toml` output filenames.

The changelog has a few more bug fixes and a "Rust API" section that I didn't read. The full text is saved at `.firecrawl/uv-changelog.md`.

**Node.js 24 ("Krypton") is the current LTS.** It gets security updates until **30 April 2028**.

- **Active LTS:** v24 is in Active LTS until about 20 October 2026, which is tomorrow. After that it moves to Maintenance LTS, which only gets critical bug fixes and security patches.
- **Security support:** it ends on 30 April 2028. After that the version is end-of-life.
- **What's next:** v26 was released on 5 May 2026 and is the Current line. It is planned to enter LTS on about 28 October 2026. If you're starting a new project this month, v24 is the safe choice, and v26 becomes the LTS pick in about a week.

I crawled the formatter section, but only 2 pages came back, not 15: `/ruff/formatter/` and `/ruff/formatter/black/`. The crawler didn't find more pages under that path. Those two pages show only a few options in examples. The full option list is on the separate `/ruff/settings/` page, which wasn't part of this crawl.

**Options these pages mention:**
- `line-length`: maximum line width. The page says formatted code may still exceed it.
- `quote-style`: the preferred quote character. The example uses `"single"`, and the page says the default is double.
- `indent-style`: spaces or tabs. The example uses `"tab"`.
- `docstring-code-format`: formats Python code examples inside docstrings, such as doctest, Markdown and reStructuredText blocks. It skips blocks that don't parse.
- `docstring-code-line-length`: line width for code inside docstrings. The example uses `20`.
- `nested-string-quote-style`: quote choice for nested f-string quotes. It's in the preview-style section, and `"preferred"` is the value shown.
- `preview`: turns on preview formatting styles, referenced as `format.preview`.
- `extend-exclude`: not a formatter option, but the page uses it to exclude files, for example `*.md`.

**Command-line flags and pragmas mentioned:**
- `ruff format --check`: reports files that would change without writing them. It exits 0 if nothing would change and 1 if something would.
- `# fmt: off`, `# fmt: on` and `# fmt: skip`: suppress formatting for statements.
- `<!-- fmt:off -->` and `<!-- fmt:on -->`: the same, inside Markdown code blocks.
- isort settings to avoid because they conflict with the formatter: `force-single-line`, `force-wrap-aliases`, `lines-after-imports`, `lines-between-types` and `split-on-trailing-comma`.

The other format options (for example `indent-width`, `line-ending`, `skip-magic-trailing-comma`) aren't documented on the two pages I got. I can scrape `/ruff/settings/` if you'd like the full list.

**Vercel gives more free bandwidth.** I scraped both pricing pages today.

| | Free-tier bandwidth |
|---|---|
| **Vercel (Hobby)** | **100 GB/month** of Fast Data Transfer, plus 1M CDN requests/month |
| **Netlify (Free)** | **About 15 GB/month at most**, and only if you spend all your credits on it |

Netlify's free plan has no fixed bandwidth allowance. It gives you a pool of 300 credits per month that all usage draws from: bandwidth, compute, production deploys and web requests. Bandwidth costs 20 credits per GB, so 300 credits works out to 15 GB if nothing else uses them. Production deploys cost 15 credits each, so a realistic site gets less than 15 GB.

Vercel's Hobby plan is limited to its usage caps and can't buy extra. On Netlify, extra credits are available only if you turn on auto-recharge, which is off by default.

Vercel's Hobby plan is also for personal, non-commercial use only.

The latest release in the changelog is **uv 0.13.2**, released 2026-10-19.

**Enhancements**
- `uv workspace metadata` now reports all installed packages, including ones outside the selected resolution.
- Exporting `pylock.toml` now includes supported environment restrictions.
- Dropped GET and HEAD requests for package and index data are now retried.
- Wheel data scripts that need shell launchers keep their encoding declarations.
- `uv python find --script` now shows causes and hints when it can't find an interpreter, including with `-q`.
- ksh activation instructions are now valid, and non-relocatable environments work under OpenBSD-derived ksh.
- uv-build's `[build-system].requires` validation now accepts PEP 508 direct URLs, including Mercurial and extensionless archive URLs.

**Python**
- Added PyPy 3.11.17 and 3.12.15.

**Preview**
- With `wheel-variants`, uv now fetches and parses PEP 825 index-level variant metadata.

**Performance**
- Complex dependency markers are handled much faster, with no exponential blowup when simplifying, traversing or exporting them. They also use less time and memory to parse and store.
- The resolver uses less memory on large dependency graphs, forks, extras and dependency groups.
- Project discovery in large workspaces is faster because member names are cached.
- The uv binary and the `uv-build` binary (including Linux x86_64 wheels) are smaller, and CycloneDX exports are faster.
- TOML parsing allocates less.

**Bug fixes**
- `--exclude-newer` is now respected when a newer wheel for the selected source distribution is already cached.
- URL credentials no longer leak through diagnostics or persisted metadata.
- Signed `--find-links` URLs that differ only in sensitive query values now get separate cache entries.
- PEP 751 environment restrictions are honored when installing or syncing from `pylock.toml`.
- `uv publish` uses configured credentials before prompting, and doesn't prompt when nothing is uploaded.
- Recursive build globs now match against complete file paths, and invalid license symlinks are ignored.
- Several panics became proper errors or were avoided:
  - an invalid `uv pip compile --python-version`
  - an invalid `pylock.toml` output filename
  - repeated resolution conflicts involving fixed-priority packages
- Version aliases are now created correctly when installing managed Python into a relative directory.
- `uv pip check` shows incompatibilities with `-q`.
- Logically equivalent dependency markers now compare as equal regardless of construction order.

**Rust API**
- Raw `url::Url` APIs in `uv-pep508` now require the opt-in `unsafe-url` feature.

I only read the first 5,000 characters of the file, so the Rust API section may have more entries after that one.

Source: https://github.com/astral-sh/uv/blob/main/CHANGELOG.md

**Node.js 24 ("Krypton")** is the current LTS as of 2026-10-19. Its security updates end on **30 April 2028**.

- Node.js 24 was first released on 6 May 2025. Its latest release is 24.22.0, from 14 Oct 2026.
- endoflife.date lists "active support" for v24 as ending on 20 Oct 2026, which is tomorrow. After that it moves to maintenance, which still gets security fixes until the April 2028 date.
- **Node.js 26** is the Current line, released 5 May 2026. It is planned to enter LTS around late October 2026 and reach end of life in April 2029. Once it does, it will replace v24 as the current LTS.
- **Node.js 22 ("Jod")** is in maintenance LTS, with security support until 30 April 2027.
- Node.js 20 is already end of life.

If you're picking a version for production today, use v24. Plan to move to v26 once it enters LTS.

Sources: [nodejs.org/en/about/previous-releases](https://nodejs.org/en/about/previous-releases), [endoflife.date/nodejs](https://endoflife.date/nodejs), and the [Node.js release schedule announcement](https://nodejs.org/en/blog/announcements/evolving-the-nodejs-release-schedule).
